title: Predicting the Slow Drift of Nuclear Spin Noise in Semiconductor Spin Qubits
authors: Wayne M. Witzel, Jesse J. Lutz, Matthew D. Grace, Natalie D. Foster, Ryan M. Jock, Dwight R. Luhman
abstract: The dynamics of a nuclear spin bath generates magnetic noise that is a key contributor to the decoherence of electron spin qubits in electrostatically-defined quantum dots. In this paper, we extend the cluster correlation expansion (CCE) technique, which has proven useful for predicting solid-state qubit coherence times across various settings but is limited to shorter time scales, to incorporate stochastic treatments of cluster dynamics in order to efficiently predict slow drifting Overhauser fields over longer time scales. This approach combines quantum evolution with classical rate matrices to enable simulation across a wide range of temporal regimes required to simulate, for example, the long-time convergence of the ergodic $T_2^*$ from Ramsey experiments. Our methodology is validated against experimental data from various silicon spin qubit systems, demonstrating a strong agreement between simulation and measurement of Ramsey experiments presented in the form of $T_2^*$ versus averaging time, autocorrelation functions, as well as power spectral densities. Furthermore, we demonstrate significant back-action effects through modeling and experiment; specifically, the dynamics of the nuclear spin bath depends upon the electron spin occupation schedule. Finally, our modeling quantitatively predicts the benefits from compensating for the slow drift of Overhauser fields in qubit operations. Our findings indicate that compensating for an Overhauser rotation measured $Δt$ in the past results in an effective $T_2^*$, which we denote $\tilde{T}_2^*(Δt)$ for clarity, under certain scenarios of interest, can be one or two orders of magnitude larger than the ergodic $T_2^*$ if the Overhauser rotation is re-characterized every 100 milliseconds; that is, $\tilde{T}_2^*(Δt = 100~{\rm ms})$ can be $10$ to $100$ times larger than $T_2^*$.
summary: This paper develops an advanced theoretical framework combining Cluster Correlation Expansion with stochastic methods to model the long-term magnetic noise from nuclear spins affecting electron spin qubits. The authors validate this approach against experimental data and show that actively compensating for the measured Overhauser field can dramatically extend qubit coherence times, offering a pathway toward more robust quantum computation in solid-state systems.
main_problem: The primary challenge is accurately predicting the slow drift of magnetic noise originating from the nuclear spin bath, which severely limits the coherence time ($T_2^*$) of electron spin qubits in semiconductor quantum dots.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that by actively compensating for the measured Overhauser field rotation ($\Delta t$), the effective coherence time $	ilde{T}_2^*$ can be significantly enhanced—potentially 10 to 100 times larger than the ergodic $T_2^*$.
method: They extend the Cluster Correlation Expansion (CCE) technique by incorporating stochastic treatments of cluster dynamics, combining quantum evolution with classical rate matrices to simulate long-time noise behavior.
model_or_system: The system involves electron spin qubits coupled to a bath of nuclear spins within semiconductor quantum dots. The Hamiltonian includes Zeeman, Fermi contact hyperfine ($H_{hf}$), and dipolar interactions ($\mathbf{D}$).
key_observables: $T_2^*$ decay time (Ramsey experiments), autocorrelation functions of the Overhauser field, and Power Spectral Densities (PSDs).
important_parameters: The simulation relies on modeling periodic electron occupation cycles ($T = t_{	ext{on}} + t_{	ext{off}}$) and quantifying noise drift over long timescales ($\mu$s regime).
main_assumptions: Key approximations include neglecting fast electronic dynamics relative to slow nuclear bath evolution, assuming low temperatures where phonon decay is negligible, and using the CCE formalism.
figures_summary: Figures validate the method by showing convergence tests for model dimensions (Fig. 12) and comparing numerical histograms of nearest-neighbor distributions against analytical results (Fig. 14).
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the physical noise source to extending the CCE technique for long timescales, validating the methodology against multiple experimental diagnostics ($T_2^*$, autocorrelation), demonstrating back-action effects, and finally quantifying the benefits of active field compensation.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a fundamental decoherence bottleneck in solid-state quantum computing platforms by providing a quantitative method to mitigate slow environmental noise sources through dynamic control.
